To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) land-use conflicts are analytically analogous to economic transactions, (2) land-use conflicts involve disputes over the institutions that govern land-use decisions, (3) land-use conflicts may be framed as transactions that involve harm, (4) land-use conflicts can be processed by institutions that are appropriate to the transaction framing, and (5) land-use conflicts that are framed as transactions that are not harmful may be resolved by market transactions, but those that are framed as harmful require dispute processing.

(1) the institutional structure of a community affects how disputes are processed and resolved; (2) the structure of institutions affects the nature of the disputes; (3) the nature of the dispute affects the structure of the institutions; and (4) the structure of the dispute affects its resolution.

land-use conflicts are transactions, that the parties involved have different interests, that these interests are affected by the institutions that are in place to process the transactions, that these institutions are affected by political forces, and that the institutions are affected by the transactions themselves.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role that institutions play in shaping the nature of land-use disputes and in determining the appropriate means of dispute processing.
the role of institutions in the processing of land-use disputes and how the institutional framework shapes the outcomes of these disputes.
how institutions are created and maintained, how they change and how their change is resisted or accepted.
